title: Annual precipitation reversal rates showed no clear change across 344 US divisions from 1901-1960 to 1966-2025
abstract: We tested whether annual precipitation reversals between local dry and wet tails changed across 344 US climate divisions. NOAA nClimDiv water-year totals gave 1,596 reversals in 1901-1960 and 1,517 in 1966-2025. With local 20th and 80th percentiles set within each period, the rate fell from 7.86% to 7.47%. The late-minus-early change was -0.39 percentage points. Its conditional 95% five-edge block interval was -2.48 to +1.74 points. A national year-field shuffle gave a two-sided p value of 0.6455 for the change relative to its exact reference mean. Pooled thresholds changed the point sign to +0.39 points, but its interval also included zero. All five planned setting checks had intervals that included zero. Thus, this annual precipitation measure did not resolve a change in reversal frequency. The result does not establish equal rates or test water-balance whiplash, flood risk, storage recovery, or a climate cause. Threshold choice, annual aggregation, source error and long climate cycles limit inference. Code, input data, derived evidence, an audit and repeat instructions are supplied.

display.caption: Annual reversal rates and conditional intervals for changes between two periods. Black marks show exact shuffled-year expectations. Intervals keep thresholds fixed. The fractions give equal weight to divisions, not land area.

citations.reason: Prior national direction test sets the context. We test a change between periods, which that study did not test. Data overlap is complete; this is not independent replication.
Source format document and national field-shuffle context.
Prior seven-division winter comparison used the same periods and a tail-count reference. We extend the scope to annual precipitation across 344 divisions; this is not a new decomposition method.
